lesson.title: Reactions That Release or Absorb Energy
lesson.subject: science

contentBlocks.text: Some chemical reactions make things feel warmer. Others make things feel colder. Today, discover why — and that both are completely normal chemistry.

An exothermic reaction releases energy (usually as heat) into its surroundings — burning wood, rusting metal (very slowly), and a car engine burning fuel are all exothermic, and you can feel the heat they release. An endothermic reaction absorbs energy from its surroundings, making things feel cooler — an instant cold pack uses an endothermic reaction, and baking soda dissolving in water absorbs a small amount of heat too, feeling slightly cool to the touch. Try this: dissolve a spoonful of baking soda in a cup of room-temperature water, and feel the outside of the cup before and after — describe what you notice.
You just investigated real energy changes in chemical reactions — exothermic and endothermic. Tomorrow we'll review everything about matter and chemical reactions from this whole week.

objectives: Distinguish exothermic reactions (release energy) from endothermic reactions (absorb energy)
Investigate a real endothermic reaction (baking soda dissolving in water) and describe observed evidence
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's chemical-reaction evidence and conservation of mass.
2. Introduce exothermic vs. endothermic with the burning/cold-pack examples.
3. Do the baking-soda-in-water investigation, feeling the cup before and after.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus on just one clear example of each type (burning = exothermic, cold pack = endothermic) rather than a longer list
Ready for more: research one more real example of each type and explain what evidence shows it's exothermic or endothermic
The baking-soda-in-water temperature change is subtle — set expectations that it's a small, gentle cooling, not a dramatic one
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Exothermic reactions release energy (heat) into their surroundings. 2. Endothermic reactions absorb energy from their surroundings. 3. Burning wood is exothermic; a cold pack is endothermic.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Connects to NGSS MS-PS1-6 (thermal energy release/absorption in chemical processes), rounding out the week's chemical-reaction unit with the energy dimension named in the course's own 'energy, matter, and chemical reactions' description.
